rosemary.region_notes_seasoned: In the Rio Grande Valley, rosemary is a true year-round evergreen perennial: winters are essentially frost-free and well within its hardy range, so there is no dieback to recover from each spring. 9.grown_as_note_seasoned: Lavender is perennial in name only in the Rio Grande Valley, and best grown in a container. Cold is not the problem this far south; the Valley's heat and humidity are genuinely hard on this dry-climate Mediterranean plant, and LSU AgCenter is blunt that lavender is a challenge across the humid Gulf South for exactly this reason: plants grow acceptably through the cooler months, but once heat and humidity build they trigger root and crown rot. English lavender largely fails in this climate; choose heat- and humidity-tolerant types such as Spanish lavender, Goodwin Creek Grey, or the hybrid Phenomenal, planted in a well-drained container so drainage and airflow can be controlled. Expect it to be short-lived and be prepared to replace plants that decline over a hot, humid stretch.

Grow it in a pot with excellent drainage and good airflow, choose a tough type like Spanish lavender or Phenomenal, and do not expect it to last for many years.

lavender.region_notes_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley is a genuinely hard climate for lavender, and honesty matters more than optimism here. 9.type_note_seasoned: Blackberry is the most viable berry crop for the Rio Grande Valley. Low-chill Texas-bred erect and semi-erect types, historically Brazos and Rosborough and now newer thornless low-chill cultivars such as Natchez, Ouachita, and Kiowa, fruit reliably in the Valley's mild winters. Texas A&M AgriLife's statewide crop survey records no commercial blackberry acreage in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, so treat this as a genuine dooryard, home-garden crop rather than a commercial one, not because it fails here but because Valley growers have not commercialized it.

9.type_note_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley is at or beyond the limit for raspberries: insufficient winter chill and intense summer heat defeat standard reds. Only a heat-tolerant, low-chill trailing type such as Dorman Red, a Texas-bred selection recommended by Texas A&M AgriLife's Master Gardener plant library, can be attempted, and only for a small early-spring crop of fair, mostly cooking-quality fruit. Treat it as a novelty, not a staple; blackberry is the far better caneberry choice here.
9.type_note_beginner: Raspberries are a tough sell in the Rio Grande Valley. Most types will not grow here at all, since the Valley does not get enough winter chill and gets too hot in summer. The one worth trying is a heat-tolerant, low-chill type called Dorman Red, and even then expect a small crop, best used for cooking, not a heavy fresh harvest. Grow blackberries instead if you want a reliable caneberry.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The Valley is essentially frost-free, so cold is not the limiting factor for raspberry here; heat and insufficient winter chill, not frost, end the season and constrain what will fruit at all.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Valley a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, heat-tolerant trailing cane fruit, planted while dormant in winter; it blooms in late winter and ripens a small early-spring crop before the worst heat arrives, then is pruned and retrained in the dormant season. Only the low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist here, and even those are best treated as a short-lived novelty rather than a dependable planting.

9.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is native to riparian habitat throughout Texas, including the Rio Grande Valley, and is a genuinely adaptable choice here; there is no separate warm-climate type as there is for blueberry. It grows and fruits in the Valley, though it wants steady moisture and benefits from some afternoon shade in the most intense summer heat. Plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
9.type_note_beginner: American elderberry is a Texas native, including along the Rio Grande, so it is a solid, adaptable choice for the Valley. It is the one common type; there is no special warm-climate version. Give it plenty of water and a little afternoon shade in the hottest part of summer, and plant two different varieties for a good crop.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The Valley is essentially frost-free, so cold is not a concern for elderberry here; keeping the plant watered through the long, intense summer heat is the real management task.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent deciduous shrub in the Valley too, planted once and kept for years, though in the mild winters here it rests only briefly. It blooms earlier than farther north and ripens earlier as well; keep it well watered through the intense summer heat, renew old canes in late winter, and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set.

9.type_note_seasoned: Blueberry is the least-suited berry crop in the Rio Grande Valley, and growers should not expect reliable fruit. Two separate problems stack here: Texas A&M AgriLife's statewide crop guidance records 0 acres of commercial blueberry production in the Lower Valley and notes rabbiteye, Texas's usual recommendation for most of the state, is grown in acid soils, while Valley soils run alkaline; and the Valley's near-zero winter chill falls short even of rabbiteye's minimum, let alone standard highbush types. The only remotely viable option is the lowest-chill southern highbush selections, grown in containers filled with an amended acidic mix, and even that is a genuine stretch, not a dependable crop.
9.type_note_beginner: Blueberry is the hardest berry to grow well in the Rio Grande Valley, and you should not expect a reliable harvest. Two things work against it: Valley soil is alkaline, and blueberries need acid soil, and Valley winters do not get cold enough even for the low-chill types normally recommended for Texas. Your best (still uncertain) shot is a very-low-chill southern highbush variety grown in a container filled with acidic potting mix, not planted in the ground.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor for blueberry in the Valley; the limiting factors are insufficient winter chill and alkaline native soil, so bloom and fruiting are erratic even with a well-chosen container planting.
9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Valley, blueberry is a niche, uncertain crop grown almost always in a container with an amended acidic mix, since native soils are alkaline and unsuited to this plant regardless of chill. Only the very lowest-chill southern highbush cultivars have any real chance, and even they may bloom and fruit erratically given how little chill the Valley banks most winters. Treat any harvest as a bonus, not an expectation, and plant more than one cultivar for better pollination.

9.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Rio Grande Valley grows strawberries as a winter annual, not a perennial bed, the same system used across the warm South. Texas A&M AgriLife's Aggie Horticulture small-acreage guide places strawberries as adapted south of Houston, San Antonio, and Del Rio, which includes the Valley, with harvest concentrated late March into early April.
